indicators.note: about signals that the letters of the two words before it are moved around into a new order

explanation.surface: A few layabouts loafing around to the sound of music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' rearranges the eight letters of SOME and IDLE; 'to' is only a link to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Tunes or airs taken together make up music, so the plural noun stands for it.

clue.text: Work in China leads to low spirits

indicators.note: in tells us one piece is placed inside the other, so the word for work sits within the porcelain

parts.note: Ming is the Chinese dynasty whose porcelain is famous china
op is short for opus, a musical work

explanation.surface: Labour in the Far East leaves a worker depressed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'China' looks like the country but is porcelain, Ming; 'in' puts OP inside it, and 'leads to' links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Being dejected and listless is gloomy brooding, the state of being down in the dumps.

parts.note: Judges 5:25 says Jael 'brought forth butter in a ... dish' to Sisera before killing him

explanation.surface: Describing the dish Jael served butter in.
explanation.walkthrough: The Song of Deborah in Judges says Jael gave Sisera butter 'in a lordly dish' before driving a tent peg through his head.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bible's adjective for the dish means grand, fit for a nobleman.

definitions.meaning: a water-finder who walks with a forked stick
Wordsworth's Laodamia speaks of 'an ampler ether, a ... air', more heavenly

explanation.surface: A water-finder who carries himself like a Lakeland poet.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading is the comparative adjective, more godlike, from Wordsworth's line in Laodamia.
explanation.definitionFit: A water-finder seeks hidden springs, and the same word is the comparative of godlike, from Wordsworth's 'ampler ether'.

indicators.note: slippy describes something sliding about, so the letters of the word beside it slide into a new order

explanation.surface: A warning to hurry up, said of creatures that look slimy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Look slippy' is British slang for hurry up; here 'slippy' also slides the letters of ELSE round, and the whole clue describes the fish.
explanation.definitionFit: These snakelike fish are notoriously slimy and hard to hold.

clue.text: Source of the sweetness of honey

definitions.text: Source of the sweetness of honey

parts.words: Source of the sweetness of honey
parts.note: Samson's riddle in Judges 14: out of the lion's carcass came honey, 'out of the eater came forth meat, and out of the ... came forth sweetness'

explanation.surface: A beekeeper wondering where honey gets its sugar.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is not about bees: it quotes Samson's riddle, where the honey came out of the carcass of a powerful lion.
explanation.definitionFit: In the riddle the mighty lion is the source of sweetness, called by the adjective for great force.

parts.note: not a racecourse but the path beside a canal where horses walked hauling barges

explanation.surface: A slow racecourse for horses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Horse-track' suggests racing, but the horses here plodded beside canals pulling barges.
explanation.definitionFit: The path along a canal bank was where horses hauled boats at walking pace.

parts.note: Macbeth says 'I have bought Golden ... from all sorts of people'

explanation.surface: The Scottish king purchased gilded things.
explanation.walkthrough: From Macbeth Act 1 Scene 7: 'I have bought Golden opinions from all sorts of people', meaning a high reputation.
explanation.definitionFit: Macbeth's golden purchases were people's good views of him, their high regard.

clue.text: Does it get the measure of logorrhoea ?

definitions.text: Does it get the measure of logorrhoea ?

parts.words: Does it get the measure of logorrhoea ?
parts.note: logorrhoea is endless talk, slangily hot air, and this device measures the fuel of that name

explanation.surface: A question whether some gauge can quantify endless chatter.
explanation.walkthrough: Logorrhoea is excessive talking, or 'gas' in slang; the meter reads the household supply of the other gas.
explanation.definitionFit: The household meter records fuel used, and idle chatter is also called gas.

clue.text: Fairy takes farewell of a London suburb

parts.note: a peri is a fairy or sprite of Persian legend
vale is Latin for goodbye

explanation.surface: A sprite says goodbye to one of the capital's outskirts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takes' joins the two pieces and 'of' leads to the definition; the feed's stray '.1' after London is not on the page.
explanation.definitionFit: Perivale is a district in the borough of Ealing, west London.

parts.note: the title of Mrs Gaskell's novel, read as the admirers who in Shakespeare's song 'Who is Silvia?' all commend her

explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare's song in The Two Gentlemen of Verona asks 'Who is Silvia? what is she, That all our ... commend her?' The italic title is Elizabeth Gaskell's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Country lads courting a girl are the pastoral suitors of old poetry, the youths who praise Silvia in the song.

clue.text: Father William, in Switzerland, gets one on the knee !

parts.note: pa is a familiar word for father
William Tell is the Swiss folk hero
a means one

explanation.surface: Dad, an Alpine archer, takes a child on his lap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Father William' tempts as the Lewis Carroll poem, but Father is PA and the Swiss William is Tell; 'gets' only joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The kneecap is the small bone that sits at the front of the knee joint.

parts.note: a choice where there is no real choice, said in Latin, meaning whether one likes it or not

explanation.walkthrough: Hobson's choice is taking what is offered or nothing; 'Classical' asks for the Latin phrase meaning 'unwilling, willing', that is, willy-nilly.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase means willy-nilly, with no say in the matter, which is the essence of a take-it-or-leave-it offer.

parts.note: Delius's orchestral interlude 'The Walk to the ... Garden', from his opera A Village Romeo and Juliet

explanation.surface: A park laid out for strolling to music.
explanation.walkthrough: The musical walk is Delius's 'The Walk to the Paradise Garden'; the garden is also Eden.
explanation.definitionFit: The Garden of Eden is the biblical blissful garden, named in the title of Delius's piece.

clue.text: Make short work of a seaman on the high-way

definitions.meaning: to cut a text down, to shorten it
a sailor on the ship's bridge, the raised walkway, is on the bridge just as one aboard is on board

explanation.surface: A sailor on the road makes a quick job of something.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading takes a-, as in 'aboard', with the bridge, the ship's raised deck and a high way over water.
explanation.definitionFit: To condense a book is to cut it short; and a sailor up on the bridge would be described with that same archaic a- prefix.

clue.text: Opportunity for top voices is for kicks !

definitions.text: Opportunity for top voices is for kicks !

parts.words: Opportunity for top voices is for kicks !
parts.note: a chance for the highest singing voices, which turns out to be a football pools bet

explanation.surface: A choirboy's big chance turns out to be done just for fun.
explanation.walkthrough: The top voices are trebles, but the kicks are football: the treble chance was a popular British football pools bet on score draws.
explanation.definitionFit: The football pools coupon offered this bet on match results, so it is a gamble on games of kicking.

clue.text: "Where shivered was fair ——'s spear, And broken was her shield !" (Scott)

definitions.text: "Where shivered was fair ——'s spear, And broken was her shield !" (Scott)

parts.words: "Where shivered was fair ——'s spear, And broken was her shield !" (Scott)
parts.note: from Scott's Marmion, lamenting the defeat at Flodden of the northern kingdom

explanation.surface: A line from Scott's poem lamenting a broken army.
explanation.walkthrough: From Marmion, on Flodden Field (1513): 'Where shivered was fair Scotland's spear, And broken was her shield!'
explanation.definitionFit: Scott's lament is for his homeland's army, cut down by the English at Flodden.

parts.note: engrossed in its legal sense of written out in a fair hand, on the parliamentary rolls

explanation.surface: People absorbed in their bread rolls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'engrossed' is not absorbed but its legal sense, written out formally; Acts of Parliament were engrossed on the Statute Rolls.
explanation.definitionFit: Acts of Parliament were the laws formally written out on the rolls.

parts.note: read not as dirty cars but as larvae, grubs, that share their name with tracked vehicles

explanation.walkthrough: 'Grubby' means like a grub: butterfly larvae, which give their name to tracked tractors and tanks.
explanation.definitionFit: Tracked tractors are named after the crawling larvae of butterflies and moths, the grubs.

parts.note: re is the word for concerning, as in a letter heading
a lease is a let, the renting of property

explanation.surface: Being excused from rent is all about the tenancy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'let' plays twice: the definition is a let-off, freedom, and 'the let' is a property tenancy.
explanation.definitionFit: Setting someone free from a duty or confinement is a discharge, a pardon.

definitions.meaning: sharply, bluntly, as in being told off
in the manner of a catch, the round sung by voices in turn

explanation.surface: Harshly, or in a way that sticks in the head.
explanation.walkthrough: A catch is a round, a song where voices come in one after another, so 'catchily' is in the manner of a round.
explanation.definitionFit: Being scolded bluntly is a sharp telling-off, and a catch is a song sung as a round.

parts.note: a word for surroundings or social setting borrowed straight from French

explanation.surface: The surroundings feel very Gallic.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is 'The environment'; the rest says the word is unmistakably a French borrowing.
explanation.definitionFit: A person's social surroundings, borrowed from the French for middle or midst.

annotationWithheld.why: Get a lute for protection: the answer is an anagram of GET A LUTE, but no clue word signals the anagram ('for' is only a link), so there is no indicator to name

parts.note: the Italian word for suddenly, used as a direction in printed music

explanation.surface: Without warning, a tune starts up.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the Italian performance direction meaning suddenly or at once, which is why the clue says it's music.
explanation.definitionFit: Italian score marking telling a player to change abruptly, at once.

clue.text: Renowned for grave citizens it gave Lucentio his being

definitions.text: Renowned for grave citizens it gave Lucentio his being

parts.words: Renowned for grave citizens it gave Lucentio his being
parts.note: Lucentio's opening speech in The Taming of the Shrew names his Tuscan birthplace

explanation.surface: A city famous for its solemn people, the birthplace of a Shakespeare suitor.
explanation.walkthrough: Lucentio opens The Taming of the Shrew: 'Pisa, renowned for grave citizens, Gave me my being'.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucentio's native city is the Tuscan town famous for its leaning tower.

clue.text: Like a body of top performers ?

definitions.text: Like a body of top performers ?

parts.words: Like a body of top performers ?
parts.note: a body here is a heavenly body, and top performers are stars

explanation.surface: Describing a company made up of the best actors.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'body' is a heavenly body and 'top performers' are stars, so the adjective meaning of the stars fits.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means relating to the stars, both celestial bodies and, punningly, leading performers.

parts.note: a libertine's dissolute career, which is also what a naturalist studies, the animals of the wild

explanation.surface: Hogarth's tale of a rake retold as a nature study.
explanation.walkthrough: A Rake's Progress is Hogarth's series of pictures of a young man's dissolute life; run as one word the phrase becomes the animals a naturalist watches.
explanation.definitionFit: A dissolute existence is a reckless life, and as one word it names untamed animals and plants.

indicators.note: badly tells us the letters of the words before it are put together wrongly, in a new order

explanation.surface: A woman performed poorly and was beaten by cleverer tactics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'badly' rearranges SHE DID; 'being' links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Dished is an informal word for defeated or thwarted, done for by a rival's tactics.

clue.text: " And winking -— begin To ope their golden eyes " (Cymbeline)

definitions.text: " And winking -— begin To ope their golden eyes " (Cymbeline)

parts.words: " And winking -— begin To ope their golden eyes " (Cymbeline)
parts.note: the song 'Hark, hark! the lark' in Cymbeline, where flowers open their golden centres at dawn

explanation.surface: A line from Shakespeare's song of flowers opening at dawn.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill the gap from the aubade 'Hark, hark! the lark' in Cymbeline: the flowers in question are marigold buds.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's word for marigold buds, the golden flowers that open in the morning sun.
